dropped_turns.text: If strikes sever command links, isolated units may defend bravely but cannot coordinate scarce ammunition or shifting threats. An attacker exploits that confusion across the island. That proves defense can unravel.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: On your isolated-units point, dispersed units are not helpless units. They can act independently, use preplanned tasks, and deny control locally. Your example shows why preparation makes Taiwan defensible.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Your weakest claim is that local denial automatically defeats conquest. Separate pockets can harass an occupier without protecting ports, homes, or national decision-making. Fragmented resistance is not a defensible island.

turns.text: Jillian, take the response.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Indefensible means no workable defense, not merely a difficult one. Taiwan can prepare its terrain, population, and forces to make attack costly and uncertain. If an attacker cannot secure control without unacceptable risk, the island is defensible.

turns.speaker: MOD

turns.text: No island facing a stronger power is ever defensible. Distance lets the stronger power choose blockade, strikes, or landing pressure while defenders wait. Taiwan faces that basic disadvantage.

turns.speaker: CON

turns.text: This island facing a stronger power is defensible. Its defenders can exploit difficult terrain and prepared positions, even while their wider situation remains grim. That still supports the motion.

turns.text: I mean the first claim as a judgment about lasting military survival, while the second describes defenses that impose costs. Both can be true because costly resistance does not produce secure defense.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that outside help may arrive slowly, but your main claim wrongly treats delay as defeat. A defender needs only prevent lasting control, and Taiwan can make control-

turns.text: How can denying lasting control matter if civilians lose fuel, communications, and safe movement first? Your standard ignores the human cost of waiting for an attacker to leave. That confirms indefensibility.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No, denying control does not ignore civilians; it protects them from imposed rule. Your human-cost premise assumes collapse is inevitable. Organized local defense preserves choices and makes conquest fail.

turns.text: Ten seconds to go in this round.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This decision turns on what indefensible actually means. Russell shows that Taiwan faces danger, isolation, and painful tradeoffs, but danger is not impossibility.
